g10-history-uh7-t1.overview: The year 1960 is called the Year of Africa because more than a dozen African countries won independence in that single year. This lesson follows the national liberation movements of North, West, East, Central and Southern Africa, with the dates, leaders and parties behind them.
objectives: Trace the national liberation movement of North Africa from Egypt to Algeria
Describe how British and French West Africa won their independence
Explain the routes to independence of East and Central Africa, including the Congo crisis
Identify the settler and Portuguese colonies that needed guerrilla war
Compare peaceful and armed paths to independence in Southern Africa
g10-history-uh7-t1.simple: By 1960 much of Africa had thrown off European colonial rule. North Africa led the way: Egypt declared formal independence in 1922, Libya in 1951, Sudan in 1956, Morocco and Tunisia in 1956, and Algeria in 1962 after a bitter guerrilla war. In West Africa the Gold Coast became Ghana in 1957 under Kwame Nkrumah, Nigeria followed in 1960, and Guinea broke from France in 1958 under Sekou Toure. East and Central Africa saw Tanganyika in 1961 under Julius Nyerere, Uganda in 1962, Kenya in 1963 under Jomo Kenyatta, and the Belgian Congo in 1960. Portugal and the white settler regimes held out in the south, so Angola, Mozambique, Zimbabwe and Namibia won freedom later through long armed struggles. Kenya's Mau Mau revolt showed how settler land seizure provoked violence.
g10-history-uh7-t1.detailed:
The Year of Africa. More than a dozen African countries gained independence in 1960, so the year is often called the Year of Africa. The first breakthrough came in North Africa, spearheaded by Egypt, which had been a protectorate of Great Britain from 1882. After the First World War a delegation of Egyptian nationalist activists led by Saad Zaghlul asked the British High Commissioner to end the protectorate over Egypt and Sudan. Demonstrations and strikes by students, the elite, civil servants, merchants, peasants, workers and religious leaders forced London to issue a unilateral declaration of Egyptian independence on 22 February 1922.

North Africa after Egypt. The Kingdom of Libya achieved independence from Italy under a United Nations trusteeship on 24 December 1951. The Egyptian Revolution of 1952 overthrew King Farouk, and its co-leader Muhammad Naguib, together with Gamal Abdel Nasser, made Sudanese independence a priority. The Anglo-Egyptian Condominium over Sudan ended on 1 January 1956. French North Africa was shaken by the French military defeat in Indo-China in 1954. Morocco's National Front, led by Sultan Mohammed V, and the Riff and Atlas revolt of 1953 pushed France to a negotiated settlement, and Morocco was proclaimed independent on 2 March 1956. Tunisia also won independence in 1956 under Habib Bourguiba of the Neo-Destour Party.

The Algerian war. Algeria was the hardest case because a relatively large number of white settlers lived there and were determined to prevent independence; they formed the Secret Armed Organization. The National Liberation Front of Algeria (FLN), led by Ahmed Ben Bella, waged a bitter guerrilla war from 1954 to 1962. A referendum followed and the people voted overwhelmingly for independence, which was proclaimed on 1 July 1962.

British West Africa. British West Africa comprised the Gold Coast (now Ghana), Nigeria, the Gambia and Sierra Leone. The Gold Coast was the first British colony in sub-Saharan Africa to become independent. The struggle began under the United Gold Coast Convention (UGCC), but in 1949 Kwame Nkrumah left it to found the Convention People's Party (CPP), and the Gold Coast became independent in 1957 as Ghana. In Nigeria the parties were divided along ethnic and regional lines: the National Council of Nigeria and Cameroon in Igbo land, the Yoruba Action Group in Yoruba country and the Northern People's Congress in Fulbe-Hausa country. The parties agreed on 1960 only in 1959, and Nigeria became independent in 1960. Sierra Leone followed in 1961 and the Gambia in 1965.

French and Portuguese West Africa. In 1958 President Charles De Gaulle held a referendum to defuse the nationalist struggles. French West and Equatorial Africa voted yes, but Guinea under Sekou Toure voted no, and the independent Republic of Guinea was proclaimed on 2 October 1958. In 1960 Cameroon, Togo, Madagascar, Dahomey, Niger, Upper Volta, Ivory Coast, Chad, Ubangi Shari, Congo, Gabon, Senegal, French Sudan and Mauritania became independent. Portugal treated its colonies as overseas provinces and held its empire by any means, so Guinea-Bissau and Cape Verde, Angola and Mozambique only overthrew Portuguese rule in 1973 and 1974 after violent, bloody and protracted wars.

East and Central Africa. Tanganyika, a British trust territory, won independence in 1961 under the Tanganyika African National Union (TANU) led by Julius Nyerere. Zanzibar became independent in 1963, and in 1964 the two formed the federation of Tanzania. Uganda became independent in 1962 under the prime ministership of Milton Obote, leading a coalition of the royalist Kabaka Yekka movement and the Uganda Peoples' Congress. Kenya's road was rougher: peasants dispossessed of their land by white settlers rose in the Mau Mau revolt between 1952 and 1955, thousands were imprisoned including Jomo Kenyatta, but KANU won 67 per cent of the vote and Kenya became independent in 1963 with Kenyatta as first president. The Belgian Congo became independent on 30 June 1960 with Patrice Lumumba as prime minister and Joseph Kasavubu as president, but Katanga under Moise Tshombe and South Kasai seceded, and Lumumba was executed on 17 January 1961. Rwanda and Burundi, Belgian mandate territories, became independent by United Nations decision in 1962.

Southern Africa and settler rule. Britain ruled Southern Rhodesia (Zimbabwe), Northern Rhodesia (Zambia), Nyasaland (Malawi), Bechuanaland (Botswana) and Basutoland (Lesotho), while Portugal held Angola and Mozambique. Zambia became independent on 24 October 1964 under Kenneth Kaunda of the United National Independence Party. Malawi became independent in 1964 under Hastings Kamuzu Banda, Basutoland (Lesotho) and Bechuanaland (Botswana) in 1966, Mauritius in 1968 and Seychelles in 1976. In Southern Rhodesia the white minority under Ian Smith declared unilateral independence in 1965, delaying majority rule until the guerrilla war of ZANU and ZAPU, led by Robert Mugabe and Joshua Nkomo, brought it in April 1980. South West Africa, held by South Africa, was fought for by SWAPO and became Namibia in 1990.

keyTerms.def: An organised political and military struggle by colonised peoples to win independence from colonial rule.
The process by which colonies gained political independence from European empires, especially after 1945.
Armed struggle fought by small mobile groups against a stronger regular army, as in Algeria from 1954 to 1962.
A territory controlled and protected by a stronger state, such as Egypt under Great Britain from 1882.
A territory administered on behalf of the United Nations or the League of Nations, such as Libya and Ruanda-Urundi.
The attempt of a region to break away and form its own state, as Katanga and South Kasai did in the Congo.
The one-sided independence declared by Ian Smith's white minority government in Southern Rhodesia in 1965.
The revolt of dispossessed Kenyan peasants against British settler rule between 1952 and 1955.

workedExamples.problem: Why was Algeria's struggle for independence longer and bloodier than Tunisia's?
workedExamples.given: In Algeria many white settlers organised in the Secret Armed Organization and the FLN led by Ahmed Ben Bella fought from 1954 to 1962. Tunisia won independence in 1956 under Habib Bourguiba and the Neo-Destour Party.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: settler colonialism. Where large numbers of European settlers took land, they resisted majority rule by force, so liberation usually took the form of a guerrilla war.
workedExamples.substitution: Algeria had a large settler population determined to prevent independence; Tunisia had a smaller settler presence and a negotiated path.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the settlers refused political change, France could not simply hand over power, so the FLN fought, and only a referendum secured independence in 1962.
workedExamples.answer: Algeria's large and hostile settler community turned decolonization into an eight-year guerrilla war, while Tunisia reached independence by negotiation in 1956.

workedExamples.problem: Explain why the Gold Coast was the first British colony in sub-Saharan Africa to gain independence.
workedExamples.given: The struggle began under the United Gold Coast Convention; in 1949 Kwame Nkrumah left it to found the Convention People's Party and the colony became independent in 1957 as Ghana.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: mass nationalism. A colony gains independence early when a single party can mobilise support across the whole territory and press one consistent demand.
workedExamples.substitution: The CPP built nationwide support, unlike Nigeria where parties were split along ethnic and regional lines.
workedExamples.calculation: A unified party produced one clear demand and one agreed date, so the Gold Coast reached independence in 1957, three years before Nigeria in 1960.
workedExamples.answer: Nationwide organisation and a single mass party under Nkrumah allowed the Gold Coast to become independent in 1957 as Ghana.

workedExamples.problem: Why did Portugal's African colonies win independence only in the mid-1970s?
workedExamples.given: Portugal regarded its colonies as overseas provinces of Portugal and maintained the policy of keeping its empire intact by any means. Guinea-Bissau and Cape Verde became free in 1973 and 1974, and Angola and Mozambique in the same period.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: colonial policy determines the form of decolonization.
workedExamples.substitution: Because Portugal refused to consider its colonies as separate territories, there was no legal or negotiated route to independence.
workedExamples.calculation: Without a negotiated route Africans had to fight, so the wars were violent and protracted, and success came only in the 1970s after Portuguese military and political collapse.
workedExamples.answer: Portugal's refusal to recognise colonies as colonies forced a long armed struggle, and independence came in 1973 and 1974.

workedExamples.problem: Account for the failure of the Katanga secession in the Congo.
workedExamples.given: After Congo independence on 30 June 1960, Katanga under Moise Tshombe and South Kasai seceded. Lumumba was executed on 17 January 1961, and the secession ended in January 1963 with the assistance of United Nations forces.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: sovereignty and territorial integrity. New states and the international community usually oppose secession because it threatens the principle of keeping existing borders.
workedExamples.substitution: The Congo government and the United Nations both opposed the break-up, while Katanga depended on outside support.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the central government and United Nations forces upheld the existing borders, the secession could not survive.
workedExamples.answer: Katanga failed because the United Nations and the Congolese state defended territorial integrity and defeated the secession by force in January 1963.

commonMistakes: Believing that all African countries won independence in 1960, when the dates actually range from 1922 to 1990.
Assuming Egypt was freed in 1952, when the unilateral declaration of Egyptian independence was issued on 22 February 1922.
Forgetting that the Gold Coast took the name Ghana when it became independent in 1957.
Thinking Kenya's independence came easily, when Mau Mau fighters were suppressed and Jomo Kenyatta was imprisoned.
Believing Morocco and Tunisia were French colonies until 1962, when both became independent in 1956.
Forgetting that Portugal's African colonies became independent only in the mid-1970s.
Mixing up Patrice Lumumba, the prime minister, with Joseph Kasavubu, the president, of the Congo.
applications: Ethiopia was never colonised and is studied as a symbol of African independence; discuss what that means for the liberation movements.
Read a map of African independence dates and list the countries that became free in the single year 1960.
Debate in class whether armed struggle or negotiation was the better route to independence, using Algeria and Ghana as examples.
Research the life of a liberation leader such as Kwame Nkrumah or Ahmed Ben Bella and present a short report.
Compare colonial borders with present-day African borders and note where border conflicts arise today.
Build a class timeline of independence for each region of Africa using the dates in the textbook.
g10-history-uh7-t1.summary: African independence came in waves, beginning with Egypt in 1922 and reaching its height in 1960, the Year of Africa. Colonies with few European settlers, such as Ghana and Tanganyika, usually won freedom through peaceful nationalism, while settler and Portuguese colonies such as Algeria, Kenya, Zimbabwe and Namibia needed long guerrilla wars. Leaders like Nkrumah, Nyerere, Kenyatta and Lumumba gave the movements their organisation and their demands.

events.text: Libya independent under a United Nations trusteeship
Sudan, Morocco and Tunisia become independent
The Gold Coast becomes Ghana under Nkrumah
Guinea breaks from France on 2 October
Year of Africa: Nigeria, the Congo and many others
Algeria on 1 July; Rwanda and Burundi
Zimbabwe wins majority rule in April

g10-history-uh7-t2.overview: Apartheid was the state policy of separate development of the races and white domination of the black majority in South Africa. This lesson traces its laws, the ANC's long struggle, the Sharpeville massacre and the transition to democracy in 1994.
objectives: Define apartheid and explain the policy of the Afrikaner National Party
Describe the laws that removed the rights of black South Africans
Trace the ANC's struggle from passive resistance to armed repression
Explain the significance of the Sharpeville massacre of 21 March 1960
Assess the role of Nelson Mandela in ending apartheid and reconciling blacks and whites
g10-history-uh7-t2.simple: South Africa was freed from British rule in 1910, and the African National Congress (ANC) was formed in 1912 to fight for the rights of black people. In 1948 the racist Afrikaner National Party came to power and introduced apartheid, which meant separate development of the races and white domination of the majority blacks by the minority whites. Apartheid denied all political rights to blacks and other non-whites and reserved 87 per cent of the land for whites. In 1952 the ANC led a campaign of passive resistance. On 21 March 1960 police fired on peaceful demonstrators at Sharpeville, killing 72 people and wounding 186. The world condemned the shooting and imposed sanctions. Nelson Mandela was jailed at Robben Island until 1990. Apartheid was abolished, one man, one vote was introduced, and in April 1994 Mandela was elected the first democratically elected president. He reconciled blacks and whites and left office in 1999, leaving a rich legacy of democratic government.
g10-history-uh7-t2.detailed:
The roots of apartheid. South Africa was freed from British rule in 1910. Two years later, in 1912, the African National Congress (ANC) was formed to struggle for the rights of the black population, and it later crystallized its demands into the call for 'One man, one vote'. In 1948 a general election brought the Afrikaner National Party to power. It was a party made up of extreme racist groups and it promoted a policy of discrimination that came to be known as apartheid.

What apartheid meant. Apartheid means the separate development of the races and the domination of the majority blacks by the minority whites. It denied all political rights to blacks and other non-whites. Under apartheid 87 per cent of all land in South Africa was reserved for whites. The racist National Party also cancelled the nominal rights the blacks used to have, passed several laws that deprived Africans of their political and human rights, and imposed rigid segregation in sports, recreational areas, schools, hospitals and buses.

Early resistance. In reaction to these repressive acts, widespread demonstrations and riots were held many times. In 1952 the ANC, led by Albert Luthuli, Oliver Tambo, Nelson Mandela and Walter Sisulu, waged a campaign of passive resistance against the various discriminatory rules. The government, however, continued with its repressive policy.

The Sharpeville massacre. On 21 March 1960 police fired on peaceful and unarmed demonstrators at Sharpeville. Seventy-two people were killed and some 186, including women and children, were wounded. The incident is remembered as the Sharpeville massacre. It aroused worldwide condemnation, and many nations enacted economic sanctions against the racist government of South Africa. In response the government arrested opposition leaders, including Nelson Mandela, and banned all-black political organizations as illegal. Mandela remained in jail at Robben Island until he was released in 1990.

The end of apartheid. The struggle of the ANC finally bore fruit. Apartheid was abolished and 'one man, one vote' was introduced in South Africa. In April 1994 Mandela won the election and held office as the first democratically elected president of the Republic of South Africa. He was able to reconcile blacks and whites in peace. In 1999 he left the presidency to the next democratically elected president, who happened to be his second in command in the ANC. Mandela has left a rich legacy of democratic government in South Africa.

keyTerms.def: The policy of separate development of the races and white domination of the majority blacks by the minority whites.
The party formed in 1912 to struggle for the rights of the black population, which later demanded one man, one vote.
The party of extreme racist groups that came to power in 1948 and introduced apartheid.
Non-violent refusal to obey unjust rules, used by the ANC in its 1952 campaign.
The killing of 72 unarmed demonstrators and the wounding of 186 by police on 21 March 1960.
The prison where Nelson Mandela was held until his release in 1990.
Economic and other penalties imposed by other nations to force a government to change its policy.
The demand for universal adult suffrage, which ended white minority rule in South Africa.

workedExamples.problem: Use the figures in the textbook to explain how apartheid entrenched white domination.
workedExamples.given: Under apartheid 87 per cent of all land in South Africa was reserved for whites, who were a minority, and all political rights were denied to blacks and other non-whites.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: institutionalized racism, in which laws and not only attitudes distribute rights and resources unequally.
workedExamples.substitution: Reserving almost nine-tenths of the land for a minority transferred wealth and livelihood to whites and pushed blacks into crowded areas.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the discrimination was written into law and backed by the state, individual goodwill could not change it; only the removal of the laws could, which is what the ANC demanded with one man, one vote.
workedExamples.answer: A legal system that reserved 87 per cent of the land and all political rights for whites shows apartheid as institutionalized, state-enforced racism.

workedExamples.problem: What made the Sharpeville massacre a turning point?
workedExamples.given: On 21 March 1960 police fired on peaceful and unarmed demonstrators at Sharpeville; 72 people were killed and 186, including women and children, were wounded.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: the turning point. An event is a turning point when it changes the scale of support or the response of outsiders.
workedExamples.substitution: The killing of peaceful protesters provoked worldwide condemnation and economic sanctions against South Africa.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the victims were unarmed, the government lost moral standing abroad, so sanctions and international pressure grew, while inside the country the opposition was banned and Mandela was jailed.
workedExamples.answer: Sharpeville turned world opinion against apartheid, brought sanctions, and hardened the government's repression until 1990.

workedExamples.problem: Explain how the ANC's demands changed between 1912 and the 1950s.
workedExamples.given: The ANC was formed in 1912 to struggle for the rights of the black population; later it crystallized its demands into a call for one man, one vote. In 1952 it waged a campaign of passive resistance under Albert Luthuli, Oliver Tambo, Nelson Mandela and Walter Sisulu.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: the development of a nationalist programme from a demand for rights to a demand for power.
workedExamples.substitution: Early appeals asked for fair treatment within the existing system, while the later call for one man, one vote challenged the whole basis of white minority rule.
workedExamples.calculation: As the state passed more repressive laws, a limited rights programme became inadequate, so the ANC moved from asking for rights to demanding universal suffrage.
workedExamples.answer: The ANC moved from seeking rights for black people to demanding full majority rule through one man, one vote.

workedExamples.problem: How did apartheid finally end, and what role did Nelson Mandela play?
workedExamples.given: Apartheid was abolished and one man, one vote introduced; Mandela, jailed at Robben Island, was released in 1990, won the April 1994 election as the first democratically elected president and reconciled blacks and whites; in 1999 he left office to his second in command in the ANC.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: negotiated transition. A divided society can move to democracy when the majority demands it and the old rulers accept a transfer of power.
workedExamples.substitution: Decades of protest, sanctions and pressure made apartheid unsustainable, and the settlement transferred power peacefully to the majority.
workedExamples.calculation: The ANC's struggle and international sanctions produced a free election in 1994, which Mandela won and then used for reconciliation rather than revenge.
workedExamples.answer: Apartheid ended through sustained protest, sanctions and negotiation, and Mandela led the 1994 transition to majority rule and reconciliation.

commonMistakes: Thinking apartheid began in 1960 with Sharpeville, when the Afrikaner National Party actually came to power in 1948.
Believing apartheid was only social separation, and ignoring that it removed political rights and reserved 87 per cent of the land for whites.
Confusing the Sharpeville massacre of 1960 with the Rwandan genocide of 1994.
Assuming Mandela was released and elected in the same year, when he was released in 1990 and elected in 1994.
Thinking the ANC was always banned, when it was formed in 1912 and banned only after Sharpeville.
Believing that one man, one vote already existed before 1994.
Forgetting that Mandela reconciled blacks and whites and left office peacefully in 1999.
applications: Discuss how a law can be unjust even when it is passed legally, using the apartheid land laws as your example.
Explain why other nations used economic sanctions against South Africa, and debate whether such pressure works.
Study Mandela's policy of reconciliation and relate it to resolving a conflict in your own community.
Compare the rigid segregation of apartheid with any form of discrimination you can observe in daily life.
Hold a class debate on whether peaceful protest or armed pressure did more to end apartheid.
Reflect on what the principle of one man, one vote means for democracy in Ethiopia today.
g10-history-uh7-t2.summary: Apartheid was a system of state-enforced racial separation introduced by the Afrikaner National Party in 1948, which denied political rights to blacks and reserved 87 per cent of the land for whites. The ANC fought it first through passive resistance and then, after the Sharpeville massacre of 21 March 1960, through decades of repression, imprisonment and international sanctions. Apartheid was abolished, one man, one vote was introduced, and in April 1994 Nelson Mandela became the first democratically elected president of South Africa.

g10-history-uh7-t3.overview: Pan-Africanism is the idea that peoples of African descent share common interests and should be unified. This lesson follows that idea from the New World to the Fifth Pan-African Congress, and from the split between the Casablanca and Monrovia Groups to the founding of the OAU in Addis Ababa in 1963 and its replacement by the African Union in 2002.
objectives: Define Pan-Africanism and trace its origin to the New World
Explain the significance of the Fifth Pan-African Congress at Manchester in 1945
Compare the Casablanca Group and the Monrovia Group
Describe the founding, aims and organs of the OAU
Assess the successes and failures of the OAU and explain why the AU replaced it
g10-history-uh7-t3.simple: Pan-Africanism is the idea that peoples of African descent have common interests and should be unified. It began in the New World in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries as part of the black liberation struggle. At the Fifth Pan-African Congress at Manchester in October 1945, African delegates dominated and focused on liberating colonized Africa. Delegates such as Kwame Nkrumah and Jomo Kenyatta soon returned home to lead their peoples to independence. African leaders later split into the Casablanca Group, which wanted a strong political union, and the Monrovia Group, which wanted a loose confederation of sovereign states. Despite the division, 32 states met at Addis Ababa from 22 to 25 May 1963 and founded the Organization of African Unity. Its greatest success was decolonization, but its failures outweighed its successes, so the African Union was launched in Durban in July 2002.
g10-history-uh7-t3.detailed:
What Pan-Africanism is. Pan-Africanism is the idea that peoples of African descent have common interests and should be unified. It originated in the New World in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries as an integral part of the black liberation struggle against white domination and exploitation. For the first time in the history of the movement, African delegates dominated the Fifth Pan-African Congress at Manchester in October 1945, where the focus of discussion was the liberation of colonized Africa.

From idea to action. Several delegates, such as Kwame Nkrumah and Jomo Kenyatta, soon left London for Africa and led their peoples into independence. The pace-setter of this period was Nkrumah, who also played a pivotal role in the formation of the short-lived and loose Union of African States, sometimes called the Ghana-Guinea-Mali Union. It was formed in 1958 by Ghana and Guinea as the Union of Independent African States, Mali joined in 1960, and it disbanded in 1963.

Two rival groups. African leaders became divided into opposing camps over the future of integration. In 1961 Ghana, Guinea, Egypt, Mali, Morocco, Libya and the Algerian government-in-exile formed the Casablanca Group. The remaining former French colonies plus Nigeria, Ethiopia, Liberia and Sierra Leone formed the Monrovia Group. The Casablanca Group favoured a strong political union along the lines of Nkrumah's United States of Africa, built on centralized continental economic planning, a continental defence and security system and cultural restoration. The Monrovia Group favoured a loose confederation of independent sovereign African states that would promote voluntary participation and cooperation in cultural exchanges and economic interaction. The Brazzaville group of moderate Francophone states, such as Ivory Coast, Gabon, Niger, Senegal, Upper Volta and Mauritania, joined the Monrovia Group and formed its hard core. Ethiopia and Liberia, which were neutral towards the rivalry, played a pivotal role in bridging the gulf between the two blocs.

The founding of the OAU. Despite this division, African states came together at Addis Ababa and established the Organization of African Unity in May 1963. Between 22 and 25 May 1963, delegates from 32 African countries convened in the Ethiopian capital of Addis Ababa. The main objectives of the OAU were to rid the continent of the remaining vestiges of colonization and apartheid, to promote unity and solidarity amongst the African states, to coordinate and intensify cooperation for development, to safeguard the sovereignty and territorial integrity of member states, and to promote international cooperation.

The principal institutions. The Assembly of the Heads of State and Government was the supreme organ and met once a year in a different capital city, though it could also meet in extraordinary session. The Council of Ministers normally met twice a year or in special sessions; it was subordinate to the Assembly and its principal responsibility was preparing the Assembly's agenda. The General Secretariat was headed by a secretary-general appointed by the Assembly and was responsible for the administration of the OAU.

Successes and failures. The OAU had a mixed record. Its greatest success was decolonization: it played a pivotal role in eradicating colonialism and white minority rule in Africa. Overall, however, the failures of the OAU outweighed its successes. Its major failing was its inability to bring peace, prosperity, security and stability to Africa. Its powers were too weak and its influence inadequate to deal with internal and external conflicts, poor governance, human rights abuses, poverty and underdevelopment. It was also considered incapable of meeting the challenges of globalization.

Reform and the African Union. By the end of the twentieth century a comprehensive reform became imperative, and African leaders decided to launch a new organization, the African Union. The AU was officially launched in July 2002 in Durban, South Africa.

keyTerms.def: The idea that peoples of African descent have common interests and should be unified.
The congress held at Manchester in October 1945, where African delegates dominated and focused on liberating colonized Africa.
The 1961 group of militant pan-Africanist states that favoured a strong political union along the lines of a United States of Africa.
The 1961 group of states that favoured a loose confederation of independent sovereign African states and voluntary cooperation.
The continental organization founded at Addis Ababa in May 1963 to end colonization, promote unity and safeguard sovereignty.

The OAU organ subordinate to the Assembly, which met twice a year and prepared the Assembly's agenda.

workedExamples.problem: Distinguish the two visions of African unity on the eve of the OAU.
workedExamples.given: In 1961 Ghana, Guinea, Egypt, Mali, Morocco, Libya and the Algerian government-in-exile formed the Casablanca Group, while the remaining former French colonies plus Nigeria, Ethiopia, Liberia and Sierra Leone formed the Monrovia Group.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: federalism versus confederation, that is, a single strong state against a league of sovereign states.
workedExamples.substitution: The Casablanca Group favoured a strong political union along Nkrumah's idea of a United States of Africa, and the Monrovia Group favoured a loose confederation with voluntary cooperation.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the two groups wanted different levels of integration, the compromise reached at Addis Ababa in May 1963 produced a loose organization of independent states rather than a single state.
workedExamples.answer: The Casablanca Group sought a strong political union and the Monrovia Group a loose confederation, and the OAU adopted the looser model.

workedExamples.problem: Why did Ethiopia and Liberia matter in bridging the Casablanca and Monrovia Groups?
workedExamples.given: Ethiopia and Liberia were neutral towards the rivalry between the two groups and played a pivotal role in bridging the gulf between the rival blocs, and the OAU was founded in Addis Ababa.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: mediation by neutral states in international bargaining.
workedExamples.substitution: Because neither state belonged firmly to a bloc, both could talk to each side and host the founding meeting.
workedExamples.calculation: Their neutrality lowered suspicion between the camps, and locating the founding conference at Addis Ababa underlined that neutral role and made agreement possible.
workedExamples.answer: As neutral states, Ethiopia and Liberia mediated between the two blocs, which made the OAU's foundation at Addis Ababa possible.

workedExamples.problem: Assess the record of the OAU using the judgement of the textbook.
workedExamples.given: Its greatest success was decolonization, and it played a pivotal role in eradicating colonialism and white minority rule. Its major failing was its inability to bring peace, prosperity, security and stability, and overall the failures outweighed the successes.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: evaluating an institution by measuring its stated aims against its actual results.
workedExamples.substitution: The aim of ending colonial rule was largely met, while the aims of peace, security and development were not.
workedExamples.calculation: Measuring results against aims shows one big success and several major failures, which is why comprehensive reform became imperative and the AU was launched in Durban in July 2002.
workedExamples.answer: The OAU succeeded on decolonization but failed on peace, prosperity and stability, so it was replaced by the African Union in 2002.

workedExamples.problem: Explain the link between Pan-Africanism and the founding of the OAU.
workedExamples.given: Pan-Africanism holds that peoples of African descent have common interests and should be unified; it began in the New World in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and African delegates dominated the Fifth Pan-African Congress at Manchester in October 1945.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: the translation of an ideology into an institution.
workedExamples.substitution: The Manchester Congress set the liberation of colonized Africa as its focus, and delegates such as Nkrumah and Kenyatta took the idea home and led their peoples to independence.
workedExamples.calculation: As territories became independent in the late 1950s and early 1960s, the shared Pan-African idea was given an institutional form, the OAU, in May 1963.
workedExamples.answer: The OAU was the institutional expression of Pan-Africanism once enough African states had won independence to act together.

commonMistakes: Thinking the OAU was created in 1963 as a strong union with a single army and currency, when it was a loose organization of sovereign states.
Confusing the OAU, founded in 1963 at Addis Ababa, with the African Union, launched in 2002 at Durban.
Believing the Casablanca and Monrovia Groups had the same aims, when one wanted a strong political union and the other a loose confederation.
Saying Pan-Africanism began in Africa, when the textbook places its origin in the New World in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.
Assuming the OAU succeeded in bringing peace and prosperity, when its failures outweighed its successes.
Forgetting that delegates from 32 African countries founded the OAU between 22 and 25 May 1963.

g10-history-uh7-t3.summary: Pan-Africanism, the belief that peoples of African descent share common interests, grew from the New World into a movement whose Fifth Congress at Manchester in 1945 gave priority to liberating colonized Africa. After the Casablanca and Monrovia Groups split over how closely Africa should unite, 32 states founded the OAU at Addis Ababa in May 1963. The OAU's greatest success was decolonization, but it failed to bring peace, prosperity, security and stability, so it was replaced by the African Union, launched at Durban in July 2002.

g10-history-uh7-t4.overview: Political independence did not bring economic independence. This lesson examines the features of Africa's post-independence economy, the problem of debt, drought and adverse terms of trade, and the Regional Economic Communities built to integrate African economies.
objectives: Identify the salient features of the post-independence economy of Africa
Explain how debt, drought and adverse terms of trade weakened African economies
Describe the role of the IMF and World Bank in African development
List the major Regional Economic Communities of Africa
Explain how regional integration is meant to lead to a continental African Economic Community
g10-history-uh7-t4.simple: Africa achieved substantial economic growth from 1965 to 1974, but after that there was a downward trend. There was a modest recovery in the second half of the 1990s, but it was not enough to raise per capita incomes or reduce poverty, because growth barely kept pace with rapid population growth. Two principal factors hurt African development in the 1980s and 1990s: international debt and drought. At the root of the problem were adverse terms of trade, since Africa's raw material exports dropped in price ten or twenty times compared with manufactured imports. Running out of foreign exchange, governments turned to the IMF and World Bank, whose priorities reflected the interests of the capitalist west. To integrate their economies, African states created Regional Economic Communities such as COMESA, ECOWAS, IGAD and SADC, which are meant to build the wider African Economic Community established under the Abuja Treaty of 1991.
g10-history-uh7-t4.detailed:
Growth and decline. Africa achieved substantial economic growth from 1965 to 1974, but there has been a downward trend after that. There was a modest recovery in the second half of the 1990s, but not enough to translate into meaningful increases in per capita incomes or a reduction in poverty. Gross domestic product growth has barely kept pace with the high rate of population growth, so achieving and maintaining reasonable real growth rates remains a major challenge for sub-Saharan Africa.

Debt and drought. Two of the principal factors adversely affecting African development in the 1980s and 1990s were international debt and drought. At the root of the problem are the continuing adverse terms of trade. Since the 1960s, Africa's raw material exports have dropped in price ten or twenty times compared with manufactured imports. Running out of foreign exchange, governments had to turn to the IMF for emergency foreign exchange and for further loans to help pay the interest on loans that were already too large to pay off.

The lenders and their interests. The trouble is that the IMF and its associate, the World Bank, are financed by the banks of the developed capitalist economies of Western Europe and the United States. Their priorities reflected the interests of the capitalist west, which still regarded Africa primarily as the source of raw materials for its developed industries. Borrowing therefore relieved the immediate shortage of foreign exchange but did not remove the underlying dependence.

Regional Economic Communities. Regional Economic Communities are established in different regions of Africa. Their purpose is to facilitate regional economic integration between members of the individual regions and, through the wider African Economic Community, to promote eventual continental integration. The African Economic Community was established under the Abuja Treaty of 1991, while the 1980 Lagos Plan of Action for the Development of Africa and the Abuja Treaty both proposed the creation of the Regional Economic Communities as the basis for wider integration. The communities are increasingly involved in coordinating the interests of African Union member states in wider areas such as peace and security, development and governance.

The major communities. The Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA) is a regional economic community with twenty-one member states stretching from Tunisia to Swaziland, formed in December 1994 to replace a Preferential Trade Area that had existed since 1981. The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) includes Benin, Burkina Faso, Cape Verde, Cote d'Ivoire, Gambia, Ghana, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Liberia, Mali, Niger, Nigeria, Senegal, Sierra Leone and Togo. The Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) includes Ethiopia, Sudan, South Sudan, Eritrea, Kenya, Uganda and Djibouti. The Southern African Development Community (SADC) includes Angola, Botswana, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Swaziland, the United Republic of Tanzania, Zambia, Zimbabwe, South Africa and the Republic of Congo.

workedExamples.problem: Using the trade figures in the textbook, explain why African economies struggled after 1974.
workedExamples.given: Africa grew substantially from 1965 to 1974 with a downward trend afterwards, and since the 1960s Africa's raw material exports dropped in price ten or twenty times compared with manufactured imports.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: adverse terms of trade, the ratio between the price of what a country exports and the price of what it imports.
workedExamples.substitution: If raw material prices fall ten or twenty times relative to manufactured goods, the same exports buy far fewer imports.
workedExamples.calculation: Africa therefore earned less foreign exchange, ran into debt, and had to borrow from the IMF to pay interest, which kept the continent dependent and poor.
workedExamples.answer: Falling raw material prices relative to manufactured imports shrank Africa's earnings, deepened debt and blocked economic independence.

workedExamples.problem: Why did African governments turn to the IMF and the World Bank, and why was this criticized?
workedExamples.given: Running out of foreign exchange, governments turned to the IMF for emergency foreign exchange and further loans. The IMF and the World Bank were financed by the banks of Western Europe and the United States, whose priorities reflected the interests of the capitalist west.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: neo-colonial dependency, in which formal independence does not end economic dependence.
workedExamples.substitution: A shortage of foreign exchange forced borrowing, and the lenders' priorities favoured the west's need for cheap raw materials.
workedExamples.calculation: Borrowing solved the immediate shortage but kept decisions about African economies in foreign hands, so the debt postponed rather than achieved economic independence.
workedExamples.answer: They borrowed to survive a foreign exchange crisis, but the western priorities of the lenders deepened dependence rather than ending it.

workedExamples.problem: What is the purpose of the Regional Economic Communities and how do they connect to continental integration?
workedExamples.given: The communities aim to facilitate regional integration and, through the wider African Economic Community, to promote eventual continental integration. The 1980 Lagos Plan of Action and the Abuja Treaty of 1991 proposed them.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: integration by stages, moving from regional to continental level.
workedExamples.substitution: COMESA, ECOWAS, IGAD and SADC each integrate a region, and together they are meant to form the African Economic Community.
workedExamples.calculation: Because a single continental union was not yet practical, the plan begins with regional markets that can later be joined into one.
workedExamples.answer: The communities are building blocks that integrate individual regions first and are meant to lead to a continental African Economic Community.

workedExamples.problem: Compare COMESA with IGAD using the membership lists in the textbook.
workedExamples.given: COMESA has twenty-one member states from Tunisia to Swaziland and was formed in December 1994, replacing a Preferential Trade Area that existed since 1981. IGAD members include Ethiopia, Sudan, South Sudan, Eritrea, Kenya, Uganda and Djibouti.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: comparing regional organizations by membership, size and purpose.
workedExamples.substitution: COMESA is very large and spans the eastern and southern parts of the continent, while IGAD is smaller and concentrated in the Horn of Africa.
workedExamples.calculation: A bigger membership widens the market but makes agreement harder, while a smaller group in a troubled region can focus on shared security and development problems.
workedExamples.answer: COMESA is the larger eastern and southern market, while IGAD is a smaller Horn of Africa group with a stronger focus on shared regional problems.

To overcome this dependence, African states formed Regional Economic Communities such as COMESA, ECOWAS, IGAD and SADC, intended as building blocks for the continental African Economic Community established under the Abuja Treaty of 1991.

g10-history-uh7-t5.overview: Independent African states faced ethnic and border conflicts, poverty, disease and climate stress, and the 1980s became known as the lost decade. This lesson examines those major issues and the democratic reforms of the 1990s, often called Africa's second independence.
objectives: Identify the major challenges faced by post-independence African states
Explain how ethnic and border conflicts led to civil wars such as the Biafra War
Describe the causes and consequences of the Rwandan genocide of 1994
Explain the causes of poverty in Africa, including population growth, war, climate, disease and weak infrastructure
Assess the democratic reforms of the 1990s as Africa's second independence
g10-history-uh7-t5.simple: Most African countries were products of colonialism and kept strong ties with their former colonial masters, a situation called the colonial hangover. They faced contested boundaries, ethnicity, corruption, nepotism and client-patron relations, and conflicts over colonial borders were frequent. Ethnic oppression bred civil wars, such as the Biafra War in Nigeria, which began shortly after independence, and the Rwandan genocide of April to July 1994, in which about 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, were killed. Poverty had many causes: rapid population growth, war and crises, harsh climatic conditions, diseases such as AIDS, malaria and Ebola, and weak agricultural infrastructure. In 2013, of the world's 20 war-related conflicts, 11 were in sub-Saharan Africa. Yet there was hope: in the 1990s profound democratic reforms swept the continent, ending single-party dictatorships and military rule, and this was called the second independence. The 1980s had been the lost decade.
g10-history-uh7-t5.detailed:
The colonial hangover. Most African countries, which were products of colonialism, have stronger ties with their former colonial masters. They are coming to terms with post-colonial challenges ranging from contested boundaries, ethnicity, corruption and nepotism to client-patron relations. The so-called colonial hangover is deeply embedded. France, for instance, has always maintained strong ties with its former colonies in sub-Saharan Africa, aimed at sustaining its neo-colonial grip on these countries.

Ethnic and border conflicts. Most of the newly independent African countries share peoples who belong to the same ethnic groups, which has led some African states to try to redraw colonial boundaries following ethnic settlements. As a result, Africa has seen frequent border conflicts. Ethnic oppression and conflicts within African states have bred civil wars, and at the root of the ethnic conflicts have been political, economic and social injustices. The continent has been continually plagued by the effects of ethnic conflict, from the conflict between the southern Igbo and the northern Hausa in the Biafra War to the ethnic cleansings in Darfur and Rwanda.

The Biafra War. The Biafra War, also known as the Nigerian Civil War, began shortly after Nigeria gained independence. During British rule the northern region of Nigeria was largely isolated from the southern and eastern regions, and the distribution of wealth was unequal, since the Igbo of the south-east had greater prosperity from palm oil and petroleum resources. Compared with the Hausa in the north and the Yoruba in the south-west, the south-eastern Igbo were geographically isolated, and because of their location, wealth and religion they were marginalized and labelled as outsiders. As a result of the 1966 military coup, Nigeria was thrown into a bloody civil war, and the Hausa-controlled government mobilized drastic measures to eliminate the Igbo population, which had chosen to secede and form the nation of Biafra.

The Rwandan genocide. Rwanda has a long history of ethnic conflict. The most horrific display of violence occurred from April to July 1994 between two of Rwanda's ethnic groups, the Tutsi and the Hutu. The Rwandan Genocide, as it came to be known, was one of the bloodiest ethnic conflicts in history. The attempted extermination of the Tutsi by the Hutu people resulted in 800,000 deaths, the majority being Tutsi.

The causes of poverty. Extreme poverty in Africa has many closely linked causes. Rapid population growth reduces per capita income growth and well-being, increases landlessness in densely populated areas, and harms child health and education. War and crises also deepen poverty: of the world's 20 war-related conflicts in 2013, 11 alone were fought on the African continent, all in sub-Saharan Africa, including the wars in Sudan and South Sudan, Somalia, Nigeria, Mali, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Central African Republic. In crisis regions agricultural production usually comes to a standstill and many people flee and depend on outside help.

Climate, disease and infrastructure. The African continent has suffered more and more from climate change, as devastating floods and extraordinary drought lead to crop failures, hunger crises and famine, particularly in East Africa and the Sahel region. Diseases such as AIDS, malaria and Ebola are both a cause and a result of poverty: a low level of education and inadequate medical care mean that diseases spread faster and cannot be treated, life expectancy falls and the number of orphans rises, and the loss of labour hits agriculture and food production. In many regions agriculture also lacks infrastructure and expertise such as roads, wells, irrigation systems, storage facilities and machinery, which makes local self-help so important in fighting poverty.

Glimmers of hope. Despite negative impressions of Africa as the arena of dictators and despots, there are glimmers of hope and optimism. The past two decades have seen a steady expansion of the frontiers of liberal democracy in Africa. By the 1990s profound democratic reforms had swept across the whole continent, including South Africa, where the white-settler apartheid system collapsed in favour of multi-party democracy. From Algeria to the Democratic Republic of Congo and from Benin to Kenya, democratic reforms led to the collapse of decades of single-party dictatorships and military rule. Africa's democratic wave of the 1990s and 2000s has been termed the second independence, reminiscent of the anti-colonial struggles of the 1950s and 1960s. The problems of the newly independent states reached a climax in the 1980s, often known as the lost decade.

keyTerms.def: The deeply embedded post-colonial ties and challenges that keep former colonies dependent on their former rulers.
Conflict between ethnic groups, rooted in political, economic and social injustices.
The Nigerian Civil War, in which the south-eastern Igbo seceded and formed the nation of Biafra.
The attempted extermination of the Tutsi by the Hutu from April to July 1994, which killed 800,000 people.
The deliberate attempt to destroy an ethnic group, as in Rwanda in 1994.
The democratic wave of the 1990s and 2000s that ended single-party dictatorships and military rule in Africa.
The name often given to the 1980s, when Africa's problems of conflict, debt, drought and famine reached a climax.
Continued foreign control of a formally independent country, for example through strong ties with the former colonial master.

workedExamples.problem: Analyse the causes of the Biafra War.
workedExamples.given: The northern region of Nigeria was largely isolated from the southern and eastern regions; wealth was unequal, and the south-eastern Igbo were prosperous from palm oil and petroleum but marginalized and labelled outsiders; the 1966 military coup was followed by measures to eliminate the Igbo, who seceded as Biafra.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: ethnicity combined with unequal development. Ethnic conflict becomes civil war when political power and economic wealth are distributed very unequally between groups.
workedExamples.substitution: Regional isolation and unequal wealth created resentment, a coup destroyed the political balance, and the Igbo were pushed out of the nation.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the Igbo were both resented and excluded, and because control of the state and oil wealth was at stake, the dispute turned into a full civil war.
workedExamples.answer: The Biafra War grew from ethnic division plus unequal wealth and political exclusion, sharpened by the 1966 military coup.

workedExamples.problem: Explain why the Rwandan genocide of 1994 is described as one of the bloodiest ethnic conflicts in history.
workedExamples.given: The violence occurred from April to July 1994 between the Tutsi and the Hutu, and the attempted extermination of the Tutsi by the Hutu resulted in 800,000 deaths, the majority being Tutsi.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: genocide, the deliberate attempt to destroy an ethnic group.
workedExamples.substitution: The killing was aimed at an entire group, not at an army, and it produced 800,000 deaths in about three months.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the victims were civilians singled out by ethnicity and the death toll was so high in so short a time, the event meets the textbook's description of one of the bloodiest ethnic conflicts in history.
workedExamples.answer: It was a deliberate attempt to exterminate the Tutsi, killing about 800,000 people between April and July 1994.

workedExamples.problem: Link rapid population growth to poverty in Africa.
workedExamples.given: Population growth is rapid despite prevention and education campaigns and developmental success cannot keep pace; it reduces per capita income growth, increases landlessness in densely populated areas, and harms child health and education.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: per capita income, which is total income divided by population.
workedExamples.substitution: If the economy grows but the population grows at least as fast, income per head barely changes and pressure on land rises.
workedExamples.calculation: The result is stagnant income per person, growing landlessness and poorer health and schooling, all of which increase poverty now and in the next generation.
workedExamples.answer: Fast population growth absorbs economic gains, reduces income per head and increases poverty, especially where land is scarce.

workedExamples.problem: Explain what is meant by Africa's second independence.
workedExamples.given: By the 1990s profound democratic reforms had swept across the continent, including South Africa; from Algeria to the DRC and from Benin to Kenya, democratic reforms led to the collapse of decades of single-party dictatorships and military rule, and this wave was termed the second independence.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: political liberation in two stages, first from foreign rule and then from domestic authoritarian rule.
workedExamples.substitution: The first independence removed European colonial control, while the second removed single-party and military governments.
workedExamples.calculation: Because both waves ended a form of domination and expanded self-rule, the democratic reforms of the 1990s and 2000s are described as a second independence.
workedExamples.answer: The second independence was the democratic wave of the 1990s and 2000s that ended single-party and military rule across Africa.

commonMistakes: Believing the Rwandan genocide happened in the 1980s, when it took place from April to July 1994.
Confusing the Biafra War in Nigeria with the Congo crisis of the 1960s.
Thinking ethnic conflict is caused only by ancient hatred, when the textbook points to political, economic and social injustices.
Assuming Africa has only problems, when the 1990s democratic reforms are described as a second independence.
Confusing the lost decade of the 1980s with the growth years of 1965 to 1974.
Believing population growth raises income per person, when it reduces per capita income.
Forgetting that disease is both a cause and a result of poverty.
applications: Discuss how unequal development between regions can feed conflict, using the Biafra case as your example.
Debate what the world community should have learned from the Rwandan genocide of 1994.
Identify one environmental problem in your area and explain how it could increase poverty.
Explain how disease and poverty reinforce each other in your own community.
Assess the progress of democratic reform in Africa since the 1990s as a second independence.
Suggest how local self-help groups could improve agricultural infrastructure such as wells and storage in your woreda.
g10-history-uh7-t5.summary: Independent African states inherited colonial boundaries and weak economies, and faced ethnic and border conflicts, corruption and neo-colonial ties, all rooted in political, economic and social injustices. The Biafra War and the Rwandan genocide of 1994 showed the human cost, while poverty was driven by rapid population growth, war, climate stress, disease and weak agricultural infrastructure; the 1980s became the lost decade. Yet the democratic reforms of the 1990s and 2000s, which ended single-party and military rule across the continent, were called Africa's second independence.

config.title: Causes of Poverty in Africa
rows: Reduces income per head and increases landlessness
Stops farming, displaces people and increases dependence on aid
Floods and drought cause crop failure, hunger and famine
AIDS, malaria and Ebola reduce labour and food production
Poor roads, wells, irrigation and storage keep yields low

pairs.q: When did the Rwandan genocide take place?
pairs.a: From April to July 1994, killing about 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi.

pairs.q: What is the Biafra War also called?
pairs.a: The Nigerian Civil War, fought shortly after Nigeria gained independence.

pairs.q: Which two regions are most affected by floods and drought?
pairs.a: East Africa and the Sahel region.

pairs.q: What is meant by the second independence?
pairs.a: The democratic reforms of the 1990s and 2000s that ended single-party and military rule.

questions.q: The Rwandan genocide took place between:
questions.explanation: The violence occurred from April to July 1994 between the Tutsi and the Hutu.

questions.q: Approximately how many people died in the Rwandan genocide?
questions.explanation: The attempted extermination of the Tutsi resulted in 800,000 deaths, the majority being Tutsi.

questions.q: The Biafra War is also known as the:
questions.explanation: The Biafra War is also known as the Nigerian Civil War.

questions.q: Of the world's 20 war-related conflicts in 2013, 11 were fought in sub-Saharan Africa.
questions.explanation: The textbook states that 11 of the world's 20 war-related conflicts in 2013 were fought in sub-Saharan Africa.

questions.q: Give two causes of poverty in Africa named in the lesson.
questions.answer: population growth|war and crises|climatic conditions|diseases|agricultural infrastructure
questions.explanation: The causes named are population growth, war and crises, climatic conditions, diseases and inadequate agricultural infrastructure.

questions.q: Which two regions are particularly affected by climate change according to the lesson?
questions.answer: east africa and the sahel|sahel|east africa
questions.explanation: East Africa and the Sahel region are particularly affected.

questions.q: Diseases such as AIDS, malaria and Ebola are described as:
options: both a cause and a result of poverty
questions.explanation: The textbook says these diseases are the cause but also the result of poverty in Africa.

questions.q: The 1980s in Africa are often called the lost decade.
questions.explanation: The problems of the newly independent countries reached a climax in the 1980s, often known as the lost decade.

questions.q: What is meant by Africa's second independence?
questions.answer: democratic reforms|1990s|collapse of single-party rule|end of military rule
questions.explanation: It was the democratic wave of the 1990s and 2000s that ended single-party dictatorships and military rule.

questions.q: According to the lesson, the root cause of ethnic conflicts in African states is:
questions.explanation: At the root of the ethnic conflicts have been political, economic and social injustices.

questions.q: Which list arranges these events in correct chronological order, earliest first?
options: Biafra War, Rwandan genocide, the second independence
Rwandan genocide, Biafra War, the second independence
The second independence, Biafra War, Rwandan genocide
Biafra War, the second independence, Rwandan genocide
questions.explanation: The Biafra War followed Nigerian independence in 1960, the Rwandan genocide was in 1994, and the democratic wave is dated to the 1990s and 2000s.
